title: Noble silence
hookLine: no talking, even no eye contact, so attention turns inward
tomorrow: A day of mindfulness at home

cards: On the first evening of many retreats, the teacher explains a rule that surprises newcomers. From tonight, no talking. That part people expect.

But also no nodding hello in the hallway, no smiling across the dining room, no notes slipped under doors, often no eye contact at all. You'll pass the same person at the tea urn for ten days and never learn their name.
It sounds cold. People who've done it usually say it was the kindest thing about the retreat.

teach.h: TALK ABOUT THE DHAMMA, OR BE SILENT.
teach.b: The phrase comes straight from the discourses. One evening the Buddha walks to a hermitage and hears monks inside, talking about the teaching. He doesn't barge in.

He waits by the door until their conversation reaches a natural pause, then coughs, knocks, and is let in. And he tells them: when you gather, there are two things to do. Talk about the dhamma, or keep noble silence.
Notice what that leaves out: gossip, complaining, idle chat. It isn't anti-talking. It's talking on purpose, or being quiet on purpose.
So why go as far as no eye contact? Because so much of social life happens without words. A glance asks, do you like me?
A smile says, I'm fine, really.

teach.h: EVEN A GLANCE PULLS ATTENTION OUT.
teach.b: Every exchange pulls attention outward, to how you're coming across. Set even that down, and attention has nowhere to go but in: the breath, the body, the busy commentary in your head. There's a kindness in it too.
Nobody has to perform. Nobody has to be friendly when they're struggling. Everyone gives everyone else room.

And there's a deeper layer. In another discourse, the monk Moggallana explains that noble silence is also a state of meditation, the second of the absorptions, where even the inner talk of thought falls quiet.

teach.h: FROM THE MOUTH, IN TO THE MIND.
teach.b: So noble silence runs from the outside in.
First the mouth. Then the eyes and hands. And sometimes, for a moment, the voice in the head.

how: On most Buddhist meditation retreats participants keep noble silence for all or most of the retreat: no speaking, and often no gestures, notes or eye contact, apart from brief meetings with the teacher.

o: quiet kept on purpose, down to the eyes, to turn inward
a vow never to speak again for the rest of life
the hush kept in a temple out of respect for monks

games.q: match each part of noble silence.
p: waited for a pause before knocking
talk about the dhamma, or be silent
silence as a state of meditation

s: noble silence means the Buddha disapproved of all talking
he named two good options when monks gather: talk about the dhamma, or keep noble silence.
on many retreats noble silence includes no eye contact
even glances pull attention outward, so they are set down too.
in one discourse, noble silence is explained as a state of meditation
Moggallana calls the second absorption, where inner talk quiets, noble silence.

games.q: you're the Buddha, arriving at a hermitage at night. inside, monks are deep in a conversation about the teaching. what do you do?
o: walk straight in and take over.
wait at the door until they pause, then knock.
games.why: in the discourse he waits outside until their talk reaches a natural pause, then coughs and knocks.

practice: Lower your eyes, soften your face, let the mouth rest; there's nobody to perform for, so let the small urge to check, reply or fill the quiet be there without acting on it.
Then listen inward, to the breath, the body and the talk in the head. If the inner voice quiets for even a moment, notice what that's like.

wordCard.voice: Noble silence. Quiet chosen on purpose: no talk, no glances, so attention can turn inward, and sometimes the mind itself grows still.

carryVoice: Your line: silence, on purpose. Not a mood, not a cold shoulder: room. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 26 (Ariyapariyesana Sutta), the Buddha at Rammaka's hermitage
Samyutta Nikaya 21.1 (Kolita Sutta), noble silence as the second jhana
